
# Filling in the Details {#sec-details}

## Gradual and Immediate Templates

### Translating Templates {.unnumbered}

So far, we've just been talking about Gradual and Immediate templates, but these are not the terms used by Actual Budget. We need a system to translate the Actual Budget-native template types to either Gradual or Immediate for use in this algorithm

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
**Immediate**

* Simple Type
* Periodic Type
* Percent Type
* Schedule Type (with `full` flag)
* Average Type
* Copy Type
:::

::: {.column}
**Gradual**

* By Type
* Schedule Type (without `full` flag)
:::
:::::

Remainder Type templates are considered separately, after all other templates have run, as they are now. Limits on categories (i.e. `up to`) function the same as they do now, also.

## Repeating Gradual Templates

## Priorities

So far, the algorithm works with groups of templates as a whole, not individual templates. Specifically for long-term templates, it's not possible to work out the contribution due to one template or another. So to implement priorities we need to work backwards. If $T_1,\dots,T_n$ are templates sorted in order of priority, and $C(\dots)$ is the function that returns the total contribution required by a specific set of templates, then the incremental effect of the last template is given by

$$C(T_1,\dots,T_{n-1},T_n) - C(T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}),$$ {#eq-priorities-generic}

the difference between the contribution amounts with and without $T_n$. This idea is pretty flexible, and can be used for any function $C$, not just this specific algorithm. So different long-term templates in the same category can be given different priorities, and the incremental effect of each template can be found easily.

One thing that is a little weird about this approach is that the amount contributed due to a template could be different depending on its position in the priority order. For example in @exm-multiple-by, if the last template, `#template 100 by 2026-10` is the highest priority template, then it is responsible for \$14.29 of contribution. But if it is the lowest priority template, then it is responsible for \$0 of contribution. But the total contribution from all three templates is the same no matter the priority order of the templates. So if you have \$120 of available funds, all three templates will succeed no matter their order. But if you have less than \$120, the priority order would affect which templates succeed and which fail.
